questions.q: How does Angular turn a component template into running code (Ivy, AOT compilation, incremental DOM), and why does that matter for bundle size and performance?
questions.a:
### Compilation
- Angular compiles templates **ahead of time** (AOT) during the build: each component gets a generated **template function** of instructions ({{ɵɵelementStart}}, {{ɵɵtext}}, {{ɵɵproperty}}) and a definition ({{ɵcmp}}) with metadata.
- **Ivy** (the compiler and runtime since Angular 9) is **locality-based**: each component compiles independently using only its own metadata and its dependencies' public definitions, enabling faster incremental builds and better tree-shaking.
- Templates are **type-checked** (strict templates) against the component class.

### Runtime model
Ivy uses an **incremental DOM**-like approach: the template function runs in **creation mode** once (creating DOM nodes) and in **update mode** on change detection, comparing bound values and updating only changed DOM properties. There is no virtual DOM diff.

### Why it matters
- Unused framework features are tree-shaken (instructions not referenced aren't bundled).
- Compile-time errors for templates (typos, wrong types) instead of runtime surprises.
- Fine-grained updates combined with signals enable targeted change detection.
- Builds now use the esbuild-based application builder for speed.

### vs React
React re-runs component functions and diffs a virtual DOM; Angular compiles templates to instructions and checks bindings; both are fast when used correctly, and Angular adds strong conventions (DI, router, forms, HTTP) in one framework.

  C --> I[Ivy instructions: create and update functions]
  I --> B[Tree-shaken bundle via esbuild]
  B --> R[Runtime executes instructions]
  R -->|first pass| D[Create DOM nodes]
  R -->|change detection| U[Update only bindings that changed]

Ivy is locality-based: per-component compilation.

questions.q: Explain Angular data binding (interpolation, property, event, two-way) and the component lifecycle hooks you actually need in modern Angular.
questions.a:
### Binding forms
| Syntax | Direction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Interpolation | component to view (text) | text content showing a property |
| Property binding {{[prop]="expr"}} | component to DOM or child input | {{[disabled]="isBusy()"}} |
| Event binding {{(event)="handler($event)"}} | view to component | {{(click)="submit()"}} |
| Two-way {{[(ngModel)]}} or {{[(value)]}} with model() | both | form fields, custom controls |
| Attribute, class, style bindings | DOM attributes | {{[class.negative]="amount() < 0"}} |

### Lifecycle hooks (modern usage)
| Hook | Use |
|---|---|
| constructor / field initialisers | inject dependencies with {{inject()}}, define signals |
| {{ngOnInit}} | rarely needed with signal inputs; still fine for one-time setup that needs inputs |
| {{ngOnChanges}} | replaced mostly by {{computed}} and {{effect}} on signal inputs |
| {{ngAfterViewInit}} / {{afterNextRender}} | DOM-dependent work (charts, focus); {{afterNextRender}} is SSR-safe |
| {{ngOnDestroy}} / {{DestroyRef.onDestroy}} | cleanup; {{takeUntilDestroyed}} for subscriptions |

### Guidance
Prefer signal inputs plus computed values over ngOnChanges logic; DOM work in afterNextRender; avoid heavy logic in templates.

questions.q: Why are standalone components now the default over NgModules? How do you structure a modern Angular application with standalone APIs?
questions.a:
### NgModule problems
Indirection (a component's dependencies declared elsewhere), shared modules importing everything (bundle bloat, unclear dependencies), harder lazy loading and tree-shaking, more boilerplate.

### Standalone (default since Angular 17, standalone: true implied since 19)
- Components, directives and pipes declare their own {{imports}}.
- Bootstrap with {{bootstrapApplication}} and providers ({{provideRouter}}, {{provideHttpClient}}, {{provideZonelessChangeDetection}}).
- Lazy loading by component or route file ({{loadComponent}}, {{loadChildren}} returning routes).
- Providers scoped at route level (environment injectors per lazy route).

### Structure for a large app
| Folder | Content |
|---|---|
| {{core/}} | app-wide singletons: auth, HTTP interceptors, error handling, configuration |
| {{shared/ui/}} | presentational components (buttons, tables, inputs), no business logic |
| {{features/<domain>/}} | feature routes, pages, feature-specific components, state, data access |
| {{data-access/}} | API clients, generated from OpenAPI |
| {{app.config.ts}}, {{app.routes.ts}} | bootstrap providers and top-level routes |
In Nx monorepos, these become libraries with enforced boundaries (q29).
pts: NgModules added indirection and bloat.
Standalone components declare their own imports.
bootstrapApplication with provider functions.
Lazy routes with route-scoped providers.

questions.q: Explain Angular's hierarchical dependency injection, the inject() function, and how provider scope (root, route, component) changes behaviour.
questions.a:
### Injectors
- **Environment injectors**: root (app-wide), plus one per lazy-loaded route with providers.
- **Element (node) injectors**: per component or directive with {{providers}} or {{viewProviders}}.
Resolution walks up the element injector tree, then the environment injectors.

### Scopes
| Provided in | Lifetime | Use |
|---|---|---|
| {{providedIn: 'root'}} | app singleton, tree-shakable | stateless services, API clients, global stores |
| route {{providers}} | per lazy route subtree | feature state that resets when leaving and re-entering a feature |
| component {{providers}} | per component instance | per-widget state (each grid has its own state service) |

### inject()
Used in field initialisers, constructors, factory functions, guards, interceptors and resolvers (functional APIs). Must run in an **injection context** (otherwise use {{runInInjectionContext}}).

### Tokens and options
{{InjectionToken}} for non-class values (config), {{multi: true}} for plugin lists, {{optional}}, {{self}}, {{skipSelf}}, {{host}} resolution modifiers, {{useFactory}} with deps.

questions.q: How does change detection work with Zone.js, what does OnPush change, and what does zoneless change detection do differently?
questions.a:
### Default (Zone.js)
Zone.js patches async APIs (events, timers, XHR, promises). After any async task, Angular runs change detection **top-down over the whole component tree**, evaluating every binding. Simple but wasteful in large apps; also runs for third-party library events.

### OnPush
A component with {{ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush}} is checked only when:
- an **input reference** changes,
- an event originates inside it or its children,
- an {{async}} pipe emits or a **signal read in the template** changes,
- it is explicitly marked ({{markForCheck}}).
Skipping unchanged subtrees makes CD proportional to what changed. Requires immutable data patterns.

### Zoneless (stable in Angular 20)
{{provideZonelessChangeDetection()}} removes Zone.js. Angular schedules change detection only when it is notified: **signal updates**, {{markForCheck}}, async pipe, template event listeners, {{ComponentRef.setInput}}. Benefits: smaller bundles, no monkey-patching, better performance and debuggability, fewer unnecessary checks. Requirement: state changes must be signal-based or explicitly notify (setTimeout callbacks mutating plain fields won't update the view).

### Signals plus OnPush
Signals read in templates mark only the consuming components dirty; combined with OnPush this gives targeted updates.

flowchart TD
  EV[Event: click, HTTP response, timer] --> Z{Zone.js app?}
  Z -->|yes| ZT[Zone notifies Angular after any async task]
  Z -->|zoneless| SG[Only signal writes, markForCheck, or template events schedule a check]
  ZT --> CD[Change detection from root]
  SG --> CD
  CD --> OP{Component OnPush?}
  OP -->|default| CK[Check component]
  OP -->|OnPush, no input change or dirty signal| SK[Skip subtree]
  OP -->|OnPush and marked dirty| CK
pts: Zone.js triggers whole-tree checks after async tasks.
OnPush checks only on input, event, async pipe, signal changes.
Zoneless relies on explicit notifications, mostly signals.
Zoneless: smaller, faster, more predictable.

questions.q: Explain Angular signals (signal, computed, effect, linkedSignal): how dependency tracking works, and when effect is the wrong tool.
questions.a:
### Primitives
- {{signal(value)}}: writable reactive value; read by calling it, update with {{set}} or {{update}}.
- {{computed(() => ...)}}: derived, **lazy and memoised**; recomputes only when dependencies change and someone reads it.
- {{effect(() => ...)}}: runs side effects when dependencies change (scheduled, not synchronous).
- {{linkedSignal}}: writable signal that resets based on a source (selected item resets when the list changes).
- {{untracked}}: read without creating a dependency.

### Dependency tracking
While a computed or effect runs, every signal read is recorded as a dependency (dynamic: only signals actually read in that run). Writes mark dependents dirty; computed values recompute on next read; templates reading signals are scheduled for refresh.

### Effect is the wrong tool when
- **Deriving state** ("when A changes, set B"): use computed or linkedSignal. Effects that write signals cause extra cycles and glitches.
- Synchronising with other signals in loops.
Effects fit: logging, analytics, syncing to localStorage or a non-Angular library (chart instance), DOM APIs outside templates.

### Equality
Signals notify on change by reference ({{Object.is}}); provide {{equal}} for custom comparisons; update immutably ({{update(list => [...list, item])}}).

  C[signal: currency] --> F
  A --> T[computed: total]
  F --> T
  T --> V[Template reads total]
  T --> E[effect: save draft]
  A -.->|set marks dependants dirty, recompute lazily on read| T
pts: signal, computed (lazy, memoised), effect, linkedSignal.
Dependencies tracked dynamically during execution.
Use computed for derivation, not effect.
Effects for side effects and external sync.
Immutable updates; custom equality when needed.

questions.q: Explain the signal-based component APIs: input(), output(), model(), viewChild()/contentChildren(). How do they improve on decorators?
questions.a:
### APIs
| API | Replaces | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| {{input()}}, {{input.required()}} | {{@Input()}} | read-only signal; transforms ({{booleanAttribute}}); aliases |
| {{output()}} | {{@Output() EventEmitter}} | lightweight emitter, {{outputFromObservable}} interop |
| {{model()}} | {{@Input}} + {{@Output}} pair for two-way binding | writable signal; parent uses {{[(value)]}} |
| {{viewChild()}}, {{viewChildren()}} | {{@ViewChild}} | signals that update as the view changes |
| {{contentChild()}}, {{contentChildren()}} | {{@ContentChild}} | same for projected content |

### Improvements
- Inputs are signals: derive with computed instead of ngOnChanges; type-safe required inputs (compile errors when missing).
- Queries as signals: no more "undefined in constructor, available in ngAfterViewInit" confusion; react to changes with computed or effect.
- Better zoneless and OnPush integration: input changes notify precisely.
- {{withComponentInputBinding()}} binds route params to inputs.

Required inputs checked at compile time.
computed instead of ngOnChanges.
Queries available as signals, no lifecycle timing issues.
Route params bound to inputs.

questions.q: Compare switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap and exhaustMap with banking examples. Which one causes duplicate payments if misused?
questions.a:
| Operator | Behaviour | Banking use |
|---|---|---|
| **switchMap** | cancels the previous inner observable when a new value arrives | type-ahead payee search, loading account details when selection changes |
| **mergeMap** | runs inner observables concurrently, no ordering | parallel independent loads (with concurrency limit) |
| **concatMap** | queues: runs one at a time in order | ordered writes (saving draft steps in sequence) |
| **exhaustMap** | ignores new values while one is running | **submit payment** button: ignore double clicks until the request completes |

### Duplicate payments
Using **mergeMap** (or concatMap) on a submit stream sends a payment per click; switchMap **cancels** the HTTP request client-side but the server may still process it, producing duplicates or unknown outcomes. **exhaustMap** plus a disabled button plus an **idempotency key** generated once per payment intent is the correct combination.

### Other notes
- switchMap for reads only; cancellation doesn't undo server effects.
- Error handling inside the inner observable ({{catchError}}) so one failure doesn't kill the outer stream.
- Use {{takeUntilDestroyed}} or the async pipe to avoid leaks.
pts: switchMap cancels; mergeMap parallel; concatMap queues; exhaustMap ignores.
exhaustMap for submit buttons.
switchMap only for reads.
Idempotency keys per payment intent.
catchError inside inner observables.
questions.ex: A payments page used mergeMap on the submit stream; impatient users double-clicked during slow responses and created duplicate transfers. exhaustMap, a disabled button and an idempotency key generated per intent removed duplicates entirely.
fu: What happens server-side when switchMap cancels?
How do you limit mergeMap concurrency?

pit: catchError on the outer stream killing it.

questions.q: Signals and RxJS overlap. When do you use each, and how do toSignal and toObservable bridge them correctly?
questions.a:
### Signals for
Synchronous, current-value state: UI state, derived values, component inputs, store state read in templates. Simple mental model, glitch-free derivation, fine-grained change detection.

### RxJS for
**Events over time and async orchestration**: HTTP with cancellation, debouncing, retries with backoff, WebSocket streams, combining multiple async sources, race handling (switchMap and exhaustMap).

### Bridges
- {{toSignal(obs$, { initialValue })}}: subscribes in an injection context, unsubscribes on destroy; provide {{initialValue}} (or {{requireSync}} for BehaviorSubject-like sources) to avoid undefined; errors are thrown when the signal is read (handle with catchError).
- {{toObservable(sig)}}: emits when the signal changes (asynchronously, after effects run); useful to drive RxJS pipelines from signal state.
- {{rxResource}} / {{resource}}: async loading tied to signal parameters (q15).
- {{outputFromObservable}} and {{outputToObservable}} for component outputs.

### Pattern
Signals at the edges (templates, state), RxJS inside for async workflows, converting once at the boundary.
pts: Signals for current state and derivation.
RxJS for events over time and async orchestration.
toSignal with initialValue; handle errors.
toObservable to drive pipelines from signals.
Convert once at the boundary.
questions.ex: A team rewrote all RxJS to signals, including debounced search with effects and manual timers; race conditions returned old results after new queries. Restoring a switchMap pipeline behind toSignal fixed ordering while keeping signal-based templates.

questions.q: Explain the built-in control flow (@if, @for, @switch, @let) and why track is mandatory in @for. What goes wrong with a bad track expression?
questions.a:
### Built-in control flow (replaces *ngIf, *ngFor, *ngSwitch)
- {{@if (cond)}} blocks with {{@else if}} and {{@else}} branches, and {{as}} aliasing.
- {{@for (item of items; track item.id)}} with an {{@empty}} block and implicit variables {{$index}}, {{$first}}, {{$last}}, {{$even}}, {{$count}}.
- {{@switch}} with {{@case}} and {{@default}}.
- {{@let}} for local template variables.
Benefits: no imports, better type narrowing, faster runtime (optimised diffing), clearer syntax.

### Why track is mandatory
Angular needs an identity per item to **reuse DOM nodes** when the array changes (reorders, inserts, removals). Without identity, it would destroy and recreate rows.

### Bad track expressions
| Expression | Problem |
|---|---|
| {{track $index}} on reorderable or filterable lists | rows bound to wrong items: input focus and component state (expanded rows, entered values) jump to other items |
| {{track item}} (object identity) with immutable updates creating new objects | every row re-created on each update: slow, loses state |
| non-unique keys | duplicated or missing rows |
Use a **stable unique id** ({{track tx.id}}).
pts: @if, @for, @switch, @let replace structural directives.
Better type narrowing and performance.
track gives DOM identity per item.
$index tracking breaks reorderable lists.
Track stable unique ids.
questions.ex: A payee list tracked by $index; after sorting, the expanded-details state and a half-typed reference field appeared under different payees, and one user nearly paid the wrong payee. Tracking by payee.id fixed it.

questions.q: How do @defer blocks work, which triggers exist, and how do you use them to cut the initial bundle of a banking dashboard?
questions.a:
### Mechanism
Content inside {{@defer}} is compiled into a **separate chunk**: its components, directives and pipes (if only used there and standalone) are loaded lazily when the trigger fires. Sub-blocks: {{@placeholder}} (shown before loading, with optional minimum time), {{@loading}} (during loading, with after and minimum), {{@error}}.

### Triggers
| Trigger | When |
|---|---|
| {{on idle}} (default) | browser idle |
| {{on viewport}} | element scrolls into view |
| {{on interaction}} | click or keydown on the placeholder or a reference |
| {{on hover}} | hover |
| {{on immediate}} | right after initial render |
| {{on timer(2s)}} | after a delay |
| {{when condition}} | a signal or expression becomes truthy |
| {{prefetch on ...}} | download early, render later |

### Dashboard use
Defer heavy, below-the-fold or optional widgets: charts (charting libraries are large), spending insights, offers, chat widgets, document viewers. Keep critical content (balances, recent transactions) eager.

### SSR and hydration
With incremental hydration, {{hydrate on ...}} triggers delay hydration of server-rendered deferred blocks.

### Pitfalls
Deferring above-the-fold content (layout shift, worse LCP), dependencies also imported eagerly elsewhere (no chunk savings), placeholders without fixed size (CLS).

  participant P as Page shell
  participant S as Server
  U->>P: open dashboard
  P-->>U: shell renders with placeholder for charts
  Note over P: defer block on viewport trigger, prefetch on idle
  P->>S: idle - prefetch charts chunk
  U->>P: scrolls charts into view
  P->>P: render deferred component from prefetched chunk
pts: @defer compiles content into lazy chunks.
Triggers: idle, viewport, interaction, hover, timer, when, prefetch.
Placeholder, loading, error sub-blocks.

questions.q: Design HTTP handling for an Angular banking app: functional interceptors (auth, correlation, errors), retries, timeouts and user-facing error handling.
questions.a:
### Interceptors (functional, order matters)
1. **Correlation**: add {{X-Request-Id}} and pass trace context for observability.
2. **Auth**: with a BFF, ensure {{withCredentials}} and the CSRF header; with tokens, attach access tokens only for your API origins.
3. **Retry**: retry **idempotent GETs** on network errors or 503 with backoff and jitter (not POSTs unless idempotency keys).
4. **Timeout**: per-request timeouts appropriate for the API.
5. **Errors**: map HTTP errors to typed application errors (problem details), handle 401 (session expired: redirect to login), 403, 409 (concurrency), 429 (rate limited with Retry-After), 5xx.

### User-facing handling
- Components show contextual errors (inline for validation, banners for page-level).
- Global {{ErrorHandler}} for unexpected errors with telemetry.
- Never show raw server messages or stack traces.

### Typing
Generate API clients from OpenAPI so request and response types match the backend.

  R --> E[error interceptor: map to app errors, 401 to re-login]
  E --> B[HttpBackend sends request]
  B --> S[API]

questions.q: Design routing for a banking portal: lazy loading, functional guards, resolvers, route input binding. Do route guards secure your app?
questions.a:
### Features
- **Lazy routes** ({{loadComponent}}, {{loadChildren}}) per feature to keep the initial bundle small; preloading strategies for likely next routes.
- **Functional guards**: {{canMatch}} (prevent loading the route's code for unauthorised users), {{canActivate}}, {{canDeactivate}} (unsaved form changes).
- **Resolvers**: fetch data before activation (use sparingly; they block navigation; often better to load in the component with skeletons).
- **Component input binding** ({{withComponentInputBinding}}): route params, query params and resolved data become inputs.
- Route-level providers for feature state.

### Do guards secure the app?
**No.** Guards are UX: they hide routes and avoid loading code for users who can't use it. All JavaScript can be read and modified; anyone can call the APIs directly. **Authorisation must be enforced on the server** for every API call. Guards complement it by preventing confusing UX and loading unnecessary code.

### Banking specifics
Session expiry handling (redirect to login with return URL), step-up routes (sensitive pages requiring recent authentication), and preserving navigation state securely.

  CA --> RS[resolver: preload payment, or let component load it]
  RS --> CMP[Component receives id as input via route binding]
  CMP --> CD[canDeactivate: unsaved form warning]

questions.q: Reactive vs template-driven forms: when do you use each? Build a typed reactive form for a payment with sync, cross-field and async validators.

|---|---|---|

| Dynamic forms | natural | awkward |
| Complex validation | cross-field and async validators in code | directives |

- **Async** validators for server checks (IBAN validation or confirmation of payee) with debouncing and {{updateOn: 'blur'}}.
- Server-side validation always repeats these checks.
- Accessible error messages linked to fields ({{aria-describedby}}).

questions.q: Explain resource(), rxResource() and httpResource(). How do they simplify async data loading with signals, and what are their limits?
questions.a:
### Purpose
Declarative async loading tied to **signal parameters**: when params change, the previous request is cancelled (abort signal) and a new one starts; status, value and error are exposed as signals.

### APIs
| API | Loader |
|---|---|
| {{resource({ params, loader })}} | Promise-based loader with {{abortSignal}} |
| {{rxResource({ params, stream })}} | Observable-based loader |
| {{httpResource(() => url or request)}} | built on HttpClient (interceptors apply), returns typed signals |

Signals exposed: {{value()}}, {{status()}} (idle, loading, reloading, resolved, error, local), {{error()}}, {{isLoading()}}, {{hasValue()}}; {{reload()}}; {{set()}} or {{update()}} for local optimistic changes.

### Benefits
Removes boilerplate (subscriptions, loading flags, race handling) for **reads**; integrates with OnPush and zoneless.

### Limits
- For **reads**; mutations (POST) still use explicit calls with exhaustMap or similar.
- Experimental status in some versions: check stability before broad adoption.
- Complex orchestration (polling with backoff, websockets) still fits RxJS better.
- Caching across components needs a store or a cache layer.
pts: Declarative signal-driven async loading.
Automatic cancellation on parameter change.
value, status, error, isLoading as signals.

questions.q: Where do memory leaks come from in Angular apps, and how do you prevent them (subscriptions, event listeners, timers, detached DOM, third-party libraries)?
questions.a:
### Common sources
| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| Unclosed subscriptions | {{interval}}, WebSocket or store subscriptions in components never unsubscribed |
| Long-lived services holding component references | callbacks registered on root services capturing components |
| DOM event listeners added manually | {{window.addEventListener}} without removal |
| Timers | {{setInterval}} not cleared |
| Third-party widgets | charts or maps not destroyed |
| Caches without bounds | in-memory caches in root services |
| Detached DOM | references to removed elements kept in arrays |

### Prevention
- **async pipe** or **toSignal** (auto-cleanup) in templates.
- {{takeUntilDestroyed()}} (in injection context) or with {{DestroyRef}}.
- {{DestroyRef.onDestroy}} for timers, listeners and third-party instances.
- {{fromEvent}} with takeUntilDestroyed instead of manual listeners, or Renderer listen returning an unlisten function.
- HTTP observables complete by themselves (no leak), but long pipelines with {{shareReplay}} without refCount can retain data.

### Detection
Chrome DevTools memory snapshots (detached nodes, retained components), navigating repeatedly between routes and watching heap growth, Angular DevTools component tree.

questions.q: NgRx Store, NgRx SignalStore, or plain services with signals: how do you choose state management for a large banking app?

### Options
| Option | Model | Strengths | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Services with signals** | {{signal}} and {{computed}} in injectable services, methods for updates | simple, minimal boilerplate, great for feature-local state | conventions needed at scale; no devtools time travel |
| **NgRx SignalStore** | {{signalStore(withState, withComputed, withMethods, withHooks)}}, entity features, rxMethod | structured, composable features, signals-native, less boilerplate than Store | another library; conventions |
| **NgRx Store** (Redux) | actions, reducers, selectors, effects | strict unidirectional flow, devtools, time travel, audit of every state change, proven at scale | boilerplate, indirection, learning curve |

### Choosing
- Most state is **server state** (accounts, transactions): use resources or a query cache, not a global store.
- **Feature state** (wizard steps, filters, selections): services with signals or SignalStore, provided at route level.
- **Cross-cutting app state** with complex event flows (trading desk with many streams, audit of every change): NgRx Store can be justified.

### Principles
Single source of truth per piece of state, immutable updates, state close to where it's used, no store for everything.

| Culprit | Fix |
|---|---|
| default change detection on large trees | OnPush, signals, zoneless |
| function calls or heavy pipes in templates evaluated every CD | computed signals or pure pipes |
| frequent events triggering CD (scroll, mousemove, websockets) | runOutsideAngular or zoneless with signals; throttle |

| layout thrashing in third-party widgets | batch DOM reads and writes; afterRender phases |
| unnecessary re-renders from new object references | immutable updates only where data changed; equality functions |
| synchronous heavy computations | web workers |

### Verify
Re-profile after each change; check INP on low-end devices (CPU throttling 4x to 6x).

No heavy functions in templates.

questions.q: A trading grid shows 10,000 rows updating several times per second and the UI is janky. Redesign it.
questions.a:
### Why it's janky
Every tick triggers change detection across thousands of rows; DOM nodes for all rows exist; each update creates new objects so every row re-renders; formatting pipes run per cell; main thread saturated, INP poor.

### Redesign
| Layer | Change |
|---|---|
| **Rendering** | virtual scrolling (CDK virtual scroll or a grid like AG Grid with row virtualisation): only visible rows (about 50) in the DOM |
| **Change detection** | OnPush plus signals or zoneless; updates mark only affected rows |
| **Data flow** | keep a keyed map of rows; apply ticks to rows by id; per-row signals so a tick updates only that row's cells |
| **Batching** | buffer ticks and apply once per animation frame ({{requestAnimationFrame}}), or throttle to 4 to 10 updates per second for human-readable display |
| **Outside Angular** | WebSocket parsing in a web worker; main thread receives compact diffs |
| **Formatting** | precompute display strings once per update; avoid pipes per cell |
| **Visual cues** | CSS classes for up or down flashes with CSS transitions (no JS animation per cell) |
| **Track** | {{track row.id}} |

### Measure
Frames per second, long tasks, INP while interacting (sorting, filtering) under live updates on a mid-range machine.
pts: Virtualise rows: only visible DOM.
OnPush with per-row signals.
Batch ticks per animation frame or throttle.
Parse feeds in web workers.
Precompute formatting; CSS for flashes.

questions.q: When does server-side rendering pay off for an Angular banking site, and how do hydration, event replay and incremental hydration work?
questions.a:
### When SSR pays off
- **Public pages** (marketing, product pages, rates, branch finder): SEO and fast first paint on mobile.
- Large apps where LCP matters for conversion (account opening funnels).
- Less valuable for authenticated dashboards (personalised data, no SEO), where a fast SPA with skeletons may suffice; SSR there adds server cost and complexity (cookies, security).

### Mechanisms
| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| SSR / prerendering (SSG) | render HTML on the server or at build time |
| **Hydration** | client reuses server DOM instead of re-rendering; attaches listeners and state |
| **Event replay** | user clicks before hydration completes are captured and replayed afterwards |
| **Incremental hydration** | {{@defer}} blocks with {{hydrate on viewport}}, {{hydrate on interaction}} hydrate only when needed: less JavaScript executed upfront |
| Hybrid rendering | per-route render mode: server, client or prerender ({{RenderMode}}) |
| Transfer state / HttpClient caching | avoid re-fetching data on the client that the server already fetched |

### Pitfalls
Browser-only APIs (window, localStorage) during SSR: use {{afterNextRender}} or platform checks; hydration mismatches from non-deterministic rendering (dates, random ids); caching personalised pages in CDNs; leaking user data between requests through singletons on the server.

  B->>A: download and boot JS
  A->>A: hydrate - reuse existing DOM, no re-render
  Note over B,A: event replay captures clicks made before hydration

questions.q: Secure an Angular banking application: XSS protections and their bypasses, CSP with Angular, authentication patterns, and what must never be in the client.
questions.a:
### XSS
Angular treats values as untrusted by default: interpolation escapes, property bindings sanitise HTML, styles and URLs. Bypasses come from **bypassSecurityTrust*** with user data, {{ElementRef.nativeElement.innerHTML}}, {{Renderer2.setProperty}} with HTML, third-party libraries manipulating DOM, and server-side template injection if mixing Angular with server-rendered templates (interpolation syntax in server-rendered user content).

### CSP
- Angular supports **nonces**: the server generates a nonce per response and sets {{ngCspNonce}} on the root element (or provides the {{CSP_NONCE}} token); Angular applies it to inline styles it creates.
- Strict CSP: {{script-src 'nonce-...' 'strict-dynamic'}}, no unsafe-eval (AOT means no runtime compilation needed), {{connect-src}} limited to your APIs.
- **Trusted Types** support to lock down DOM sinks.

### Authentication
BFF with HttpOnly SameSite cookies (no tokens in JavaScript); CSRF header requirement; idle timeouts with warnings; step-up flows for sensitive actions.

### Never in the client
Secrets (API keys with privileges), business authorisation decisions (guards are UX), sensitive data beyond what the user needs, and environment configuration that reveals internal endpoints unnecessarily.

### Other
Dependency hygiene (npm supply chain), Subresource Integrity for CDN assets, no sensitive data in localStorage, clickjacking protection.
pts: Angular sanitises by default; bypass APIs reintroduce XSS.
CSP nonces via ngCspNonce or CSP_NONCE.
Trusted Types to lock DOM sinks.
BFF cookies, CSRF header, step-up.
No secrets or authorisation decisions in the client.

questions.q: Plan the migration of a large Angular app from Zone.js to zoneless change detection. What breaks and how do you find it?
questions.a:
### What breaks
Anything that relied on Zone.js triggering change detection implicitly:
- Plain fields mutated in {{setTimeout}}, {{setInterval}}, promise callbacks or third-party callbacks.
- Subscriptions that assign to plain fields ({{subscribe(v => this.x = v)}}) in OnPush or default components.
- Libraries that expect zone stability ({{NgZone.onStable}}, {{isStable}}) for SSR or testing.
- Tests relying on {{fakeAsync}} zone behaviour.

### Steps
1. Move components to **OnPush** first (exposes most implicit dependencies while Zone.js is still there).
2. Convert state to **signals** (or async pipe / toSignal); replace manual subscriptions assigning fields.
3. Replace {{NgZone.onStable}} usages with {{afterNextRender}} or {{afterRender}}.
4. Enable {{provideZonelessChangeDetection()}} in a feature branch; run the app and tests; use the dev-mode check that flags bindings changing without notification ({{provideCheckNoChangesConfig({ exhaustive: true, interval })}}).
5. Remove Zone.js from polyfills; update tests to zoneless providers.
6. Roll out with monitoring (error rates, user reports of stale UI).

### Benefits
Smaller bundle, fewer CD cycles, cleaner stack traces, better performance with third-party code.
pts: Implicit Zone.js triggers break: timers, callbacks, field assignments.
OnPush first, then signals.
Replace onStable with afterNextRender.
Use exhaustive checkNoChanges in dev to find gaps.
Remove Zone.js polyfill; update tests; monitor.

questions.q: Design a multi-step loan application form (30+ fields, conditional sections, save and resume, server validation). How do you structure it in Angular?
questions.a:
### Structure
- **One form model** (typed FormGroup or a signal-based model) per application, split into **step sub-groups**; each step is a component receiving its sub-group.
- **Conditional sections**: enable or disable controls based on other values (self-employed shows business fields); disabled controls are excluded from validation and value.
- **Schema-driven** sections when product rules vary (config from the backend describing fields and rules), rendered by a field registry of components.

### Save and resume
- Draft saved server-side (debounced autosave on step completion and periodically), with version for optimistic concurrency.
- Resume rehydrates the form from the draft; never rely solely on localStorage (shared devices, PII).

### Validation
- Client-side for immediate feedback; **server-side authoritative** per step (affordability, eligibility); map server problem details to fields.
- Step navigation blocked until the step is valid; summary step shows all errors.

### UX and accessibility
Progress indicator, error summary with links to fields, focus management on step change, accessible labels and descriptions.

### State
A route-scoped store holding the draft id, current step, server validation state and submission status.

Conditional controls via enable and disable.

- **Native semantics first**: buttons are buttons, links are links, form controls have labels; headings in order; landmarks (main, nav).

- Session timeouts: warn with enough time and allow extension (WCAG timing).
- Amounts read correctly (currency formatting, negative values with text, not colour only).
- Authentication accessible (no cognitive tests; WCAG 2.2 accessible authentication criterion).
- Target sizes, contrast, zoom to 400% with reflow.

### Testing
Automated (axe in unit and Playwright tests), lint rules (angular-eslint template accessibility), manual keyboard and screen reader testing (NVDA, VoiceOver), and users with disabilities in research.

questions.q: Explain ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError and other change detection pitfalls. Why does it happen and how do you fix it properly?
questions.a:
### The error
In development, Angular runs a second check after each change detection pass to verify bindings didn't change. If a binding's value changed **during** the check (for example a child updates parent state in ngAfterViewInit, or a getter returns a new value each time), Angular throws the error: the view would otherwise show inconsistent data.

### Typical causes
| Cause | Proper fix |
|---|---|
| child modifies parent state during lifecycle hooks | move state to a shared signal or service; compute instead of set |
| getters returning new objects or random values | stable computed signals |
| setting values in ngAfterViewInit based on view queries | signal queries plus computed, or afterNextRender with a signal update |
| async data emitting synchronously during CD | proper async flow, toSignal |
| functions in templates with side effects | pure computed values |

### Not a fix
Wrapping in {{setTimeout}} or calling {{detectChanges}} to silence it: it hides a data-flow design problem and causes flicker.

### Other pitfalls
Mutating input objects with OnPush (no update), heavy template functions, subscriptions assigning fields in zoneless apps, and multiple sources of truth for the same state.

questions.q: Explain multicasting pitfalls (shareReplay, refCount, hot vs cold) and design a resilient WebSocket stream with reconnection in RxJS.
questions.a:
### Hot vs cold
Cold observables (HttpClient) execute per subscriber: three subscriptions mean three HTTP calls. Hot sources (WebSocket, Subject) produce regardless of subscribers.

### Multicasting
- {{share()}}: one upstream subscription for current subscribers; resets when count drops to zero (configurable).
- {{shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true })}}: replays the latest value to late subscribers; with **refCount: true** it unsubscribes upstream when nobody listens.
- Pitfall: {{shareReplay(1)}} without refCount keeps the upstream subscription (and memory) alive forever; cached HTTP errors replay too; stale data replays after logout.

### Resilient WebSocket stream
- {{webSocket()}} subject with reconnection via {{retry({ delay })}} using exponential backoff with jitter and a max delay.
- Heartbeats to detect dead connections; resubscribe to topics after reconnect.
- Expose status (connected, reconnecting) as a signal for UI.
- Pause when the tab is hidden (visibility API) to save resources.

questions.q: Integrate ASP.NET Core SignalR with an Angular app for real-time payment status and notifications. How do you handle auth, reconnection, ordering and scale?
questions.a:
### Client
- {{HubConnectionBuilder}} with {{withAutomaticReconnect}} (custom delays), connection created once in a root service.
- Auth: with a BFF, cookie authentication on the same origin; with tokens, {{accessTokenFactory}} (token in query string only for WebSockets, which is why servers must not log query strings).
- Expose hub events as signals or observables; update stores (payment status) by id and version.

### Ordering and missed messages
SignalR doesn't guarantee delivery during disconnects. On reconnect, **re-fetch state** (payments updated since last version) rather than assuming every message arrived; use versions to ignore stale updates.

### Server
- Groups per user ({{Clients.User}}) or per account; authorisation on hub methods.
- Scale-out: Azure SignalR Service or Redis backplane; sticky sessions if self-hosted without the service.
- Messages published from domain events (outbox consumer) so notifications reflect committed state.

### UX
Connection status indicator; toast for status changes; never rely on push for critical correctness (balances fetched from APIs).

questions.q: Angular releases a major version every six months. How do you keep a large app current with low risk, and what is your process for each upgrade?
questions.a:
### Cadence
Stay within supported versions (each major gets about 18 months of support: 6 active, 12 LTS). Upgrade every major (or at least yearly) so each jump is small; skipping several majors multiplies effort.

### Process per upgrade
1. Read the update guide (angular.dev/update) for the version pair; check third-party libraries' compatibility (Material, NgRx, component libraries).
2. Upgrade on a branch: {{ng update @angular/core @angular/cli}} runs **schematics** that migrate code (control flow, standalone, signal inputs, inject migrations are opt-in schematics).
3. Upgrade TypeScript, RxJS and Node versions as required.
4. Run builds, unit tests, E2E tests, visual regression tests; check bundle size and performance budgets.
5. Canary release (subset of users or internal staff), monitor errors and Web Vitals.
6. Adopt new features gradually (schematics for signal inputs, control flow), not all at once.

### Organisation
A platform or frontend enablement team owns the upgrade for shared libraries and templates; feature teams fix their areas with guidance; Renovate opens PRs; deprecations tracked.

npx ng generate @angular/core:inject

# Verify
npx ng build --configuration production && npx ng test --watch=false && npx playwright test
~~~

questions.q: How do you control bundle size and build performance in Angular (application builder, budgets, bundle analysis, dependency choices)?
questions.a:
### Builder
The esbuild and Vite based **application builder** (default since Angular 17): much faster builds, ESM output, dev server with Vite; supports SSR and prerendering in one builder.

### Budgets
{{angular.json}} budgets fail the build when bundles exceed limits (initial bundle, any component style, lazy chunks). Treat them as CI gates.

### Analysis
{{ng build --stats-json}} produces an esbuild metafile; analyse with esbuild's analyser or source-map-explorer to find large dependencies.

### Typical savings
| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| lazy routes and @defer | smaller initial bundle |
| replace heavy libraries (moment to date-fns or Intl; lodash full to per-function imports) | tens to hundreds of KB |
| standalone components (no barrel shared modules) | better tree-shaking |
| avoid importing entire icon sets | large savings |
| zoneless | about 30 KB less |
| image optimisation ({{NgOptimizedImage}}) | faster LCP |
| check CommonJS dependencies (build warnings) | ESM tree-shakes better |

### Process
Bundle size tracked per release; PRs show size diffs; dependency additions reviewed.

questions.q: Build a bank-branded design system on Angular: Material vs CDK-only, design tokens, theming (light, dark, brands), and distribution.

### Material vs CDK
| Option | When |
|---|---|
| **Angular Material** with custom theme | fast delivery, accessible components, brand fits Material's structure |

| Headless libraries (Angular Aria, Spartan) | accessibility primitives with your styling |

### Design tokens
Tokens (colours, typography, spacing, radii, elevation) defined once (Figma Tokens or JSON), transformed to CSS custom properties and SCSS; components consume tokens, never raw values. Material 3 theming uses system tokens ({{--mat-sys-*}}) and can map to brand tokens.

CSS custom properties switched by a class or attribute ({{data-theme="dark"}}), respecting {{prefers-color-scheme}}; multiple brands (white-label banking) via token sets loaded per tenant.

### Distribution
Versioned npm library (Nx + ng-packagr), Storybook documentation with accessibility checks, visual regression tests (Chromatic or Playwright screenshots), changelog and migration guides, and contribution model for product teams.

questions.q: A bank is choosing a frontend framework standard for 40 teams: Angular or React? Make the decision and explain the criteria.
questions.a:
### Criteria
| Criterion | Angular | React |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | full framework: router, forms, HTTP, DI, testing, i18n, SSR | UI library; choose router, data fetching, forms, state, meta-framework (Next.js, Remix) |
| Consistency across teams | high: one way to do most things | depends on internal standards |
| TypeScript and structure | first-class, opinionated (DI, services) | TypeScript well supported; structure by convention |
| Upgrade path | coordinated majors every 6 months with schematics | library-by-library; ecosystem churn |
| Talent pool | strong in enterprise and .NET shops | larger overall |
| Performance | signals, zoneless, SSR, hydration | concurrent rendering, compiler, RSC (via frameworks) |
| Mobile | Ionic, NativeScript | React Native (strong) |
| Long-term governance | Google-backed, predictable releases | Meta-backed, ecosystem-driven |

### Decision framing
For a bank with many .NET teams and a desire for consistency, **Angular** reduces architectural variance and fits .NET engineers' mental models (DI, services, strong typing). If the bank needs React Native code sharing for mobile, a strong existing React talent base, or Next.js-style SSR for public sites, **React** may win.

### Either way
Standardise the surrounding choices (state, data fetching, testing, design system, auth BFF), provide templates, and allow exceptions with justification. The framework choice matters less than consistency and platform support.

questions.q: Would you use micro-frontends for a banking portal built by 8 teams? Compare options (Native Federation, Module Federation, web components, iframes, monorepo modular app) and decide.
questions.a:
### Why micro-frontends
Independent deployment by teams, different release cadences, gradual migration (strangling a legacy app), or different frameworks during transitions.

### Costs
Runtime integration complexity, shared dependency versioning (Angular versions must align for shared runtime), duplicated bundles, cross-app UX consistency, routing and state sharing, testing the composed app, performance overhead.

### Options
| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Modular monolith frontend** (Nx monorepo, lazy feature libraries, one deployment) | simplest; teams own libraries; one release train or trunk-based continuous deploy |
| **Native Federation / Module Federation** | runtime loading of remotes; independent deploys; shared Angular runtime requires aligned versions |
| **Web components** (Angular Elements) | framework-agnostic boundaries; heavier; styling and state isolation challenges |
| **iframes** | strong isolation (useful for third-party or legacy apps); poor UX integration |
| Route-level composition at the edge | separate apps per path behind one domain; simple; full page loads between apps |

### Decision for 8 teams
Usually a **modular monolith** with strong boundaries and continuous deployment is enough; adopt federation only where independent deployment is truly needed (for example a legacy migration or a separately regulated product), keeping a shared design system and shell.

questions.q: Migrate a large AngularJS (1.x) banking application to modern Angular while it stays in production. What strategy and tooling do you use?
questions.a:
### Options
| Strategy | How | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Rewrite** | build new app, switch over | small apps or when UX redesign is planned |
| **Hybrid with ngUpgrade** | run AngularJS and Angular together, downgrade or upgrade components and services | large apps with code that's worth keeping |
| **Strangler by route** | new Angular app serves new routes; legacy app serves the rest behind the same domain (reverse proxy or federation shell) | when legacy code quality is low; avoids hybrid complexity |

### Recommended for most banks
**Strangler by route**: new features and rewritten areas in modern Angular, legacy pages untouched; a shared shell or reverse proxy with consistent header and navigation; session shared via the same BFF cookie. Prioritise by business value and risk (payments flows first, rarely used admin pages last or retired).

### Practicalities
- Shared design tokens so both look consistent.
- Analytics on legacy page usage to retire unused screens instead of migrating them.
- Security: AngularJS is end-of-life (no security patches since 2022): isolate it, strict CSP, plan a deadline.
- Tests: E2E coverage of legacy flows before migrating them, to verify parity.

### Ownership

questions.q: Mortgage advisers visit customers with unreliable connectivity. Design an offline-capable Angular PWA for collecting applications securely.

### Capabilities
- **Service worker** ({{@angular/service-worker}} or Workbox) caching the app shell and static assets for offline start.
- **Local data**: IndexedDB for drafts and reference data needed offline (product rules, rates snapshot with validity).
- **Background sync**: queue submissions; sync when online with retries; idempotency keys to avoid duplicates.
- **Conflict handling**: drafts versioned; server validates and can reject or request changes.

### Security
- Device management (MDM) for adviser devices, OS-level encryption.
- Minimise data stored offline; encrypt sensitive fields with keys derived from a session secret (WebCrypto, non-extractable keys); wipe after sync or timeout.
- Short offline windows (for example 24 hours) before re-authentication is required.
- Documents (ID scans) captured and uploaded promptly; not kept longer than needed.

### UX
Clear online and offline indicators, sync status per application, warnings for stale rates or product rules, and resilience to app updates while offline (versioned caches).

### Testing
Offline scenarios in Playwright (context.setOffline), sync conflict tests, update scenarios.

questions.q: Postmortem: after an Angular major upgrade, customers on older iOS Safari couldn't complete payments for 6 hours. What failed and what changes?
questions.a:
### What likely happened
The new version's default browserslist dropped or changed support for older Safari, or a polyfill or syntax (for example newer JavaScript features) was no longer transpiled; tests ran on Chromium only; monitoring didn't segment by browser; the release went to 100% at once.

### Contributing factors
- No explicit supported-browser policy tied to real customer usage.
- E2E only on Chromium; no device lab or cloud browser testing for critical journeys.
- No canary release for the frontend.
- RUM existed but alerts were not segmented by browser or OS version.
- Rollback took hours because the previous build wasn't immediately redeployable.

### Changes
| Area | Change |
|---|---|
| Browser policy | explicit browserslist based on RUM data and business decision; reviewed per upgrade |
| Testing | Playwright WebKit plus cloud real-device runs for payment journeys before release |
| Release | canary to 5% then 25% with automatic comparison of journey success by browser |
| Monitoring | journey success and JS errors segmented by browser family and version |
| Rollback | previous build redeployable in minutes (versioned assets, CDN switch) |
| Upgrade checklist | includes browser support changes in release notes |

questions.q: Add an AI assistant to an Angular banking app that streams responses. How do you design streaming UI, safety, and integration with banking actions?
questions.a:
### Architecture
Browser talks to the **BFF**, which calls the AI backend (never the LLM provider directly from the browser: no API keys in the client, central policy enforcement, logging, PII controls).

### Streaming UI
- Server-Sent Events or fetch streaming from the BFF; render tokens incrementally into a signal.
- Allow cancel (abort controller), show typing indicators, handle partial markdown safely.
- Accessibility: announce completion (not every token) via LiveAnnouncer; respect reduced motion.

### Safety
- Render model output as **untrusted**: sanitise markdown (no raw HTML), no auto-executed links, show citations to sources.
- Clear labelling as AI-generated; feedback controls.
- The assistant **proposes** actions (pay a bill, freeze card) as structured objects; the UI shows a confirmation screen with step-up authentication; the backend executes via normal APIs with authorisation.
- Rate limits and abuse protection at the BFF.

### Data
Only necessary context sent to the AI backend; conversation storage with retention and consent; no training on customer data without agreement.
pts: Browser to BFF to AI backend; no keys in the client.
Stream into signals; cancel; accessible announcements.
Treat output as untrusted; sanitise; cite sources.
Assistant proposes; user confirms with step-up; backend authorises.
Minimal data, retention, consent.
questions.ex: A prototype rendered model output as HTML and executed suggested "quick action" links directly; a prompt injection in a merchant name produced a malicious link. The production design sanitised markdown and turned actions into confirmable proposals with step-up.

questions.q: Govern a shared Angular component library used by 30 apps: versioning, breaking changes, contributions and adoption.
questions.a:
### Product mindset
The design system is a product with a team, roadmap, users (product teams) and support channels.

### Versioning
- Semantic versioning; breaking changes only in majors, aligned with Angular majors where practical.
- Deprecations announced one major ahead with console warnings in dev mode and migration schematics ({{ng update}} support via schematics in the library).
- Changelog with migration notes; release notes in the developer portal.

### Contributions
Federated contribution model: product teams propose components or changes via RFCs; core team reviews for consistency, accessibility, API design; contributors pair with core team; acceptance criteria (tests, a11y, docs, Storybook stories, visual tests).

### Adoption
Measure usage (which components, versions per app); dashboard of apps on old majors; Renovate PRs; office hours; deprecation deadlines with support.

### Quality
Accessibility tests for every component, visual regression, performance budgets per component, cross-browser tests, documentation as part of done.

Semver, deprecations a major ahead, migration schematics.
Federated contributions with RFCs and criteria.
Measure adoption; dashboards and Renovate.

questions.q: Run a modernisation programme moving 30 Angular apps to standalone, signals, new control flow and zoneless. How do you sequence it and keep delivery going?
questions.a:
### Sequence (each step independently valuable)
1. **Upgrade to a current major** in all apps (prerequisite).
2. **Standalone migration** via schematic (mechanical, low risk).
3. **Built-in control flow** via schematic.
4. **inject() migration** and signal inputs or outputs via schematics, per library.
5. **OnPush everywhere** with tests; fix mutation-based code.
6. **Signals for state** feature by feature (new code first; refactor when touching code: "boy scout" rule), resources for server data.
7. **Zoneless** per app when exhaustive checks pass.

### Keeping delivery going
- Schematics do mechanical work in small PRs per library.
- Modernise code when it is touched for features; don't stop feature work for big rewrites.
- Platform team pairs with teams and maintains lint rules that prevent old patterns in new code ({{prefer-signals}}, no {{*ngIf}} in new templates).
- Track progress per app (scorecard).

### Risks
Large mechanical PRs conflicting with feature branches (do them in quiet windows, small batches), subtle behaviour changes (OnPush), test gaps.

questions.q: How do you optimise Largest Contentful Paint and navigation feel in an Angular app with NgOptimizedImage, resource hints and the View Transitions API?
questions.a:
### Why images dominate LCP
On most banking marketing and dashboard pages the LCP element is a hero image or a large card. Typical causes of a slow LCP: the image is discovered late (lazy-loaded or set from TypeScript), it is oversized for the viewport, it competes with JavaScript for bandwidth, or it waits for a third-party origin connection.

### NgOptimizedImage
The {{NgOptimizedImage}} directive ({{ngSrc}}) enforces good defaults:
| Feature | Effect |
|---|---|
| {{priority}} on the LCP image | eager loading, {{fetchpriority="high"}}, and a preload hint when server-rendered |
| required {{width}}/{{height}} or {{fill}} | reserves space, so no layout shift (CLS) |
| automatic {{srcset}} via an image loader (CDN) | the browser downloads a size that fits the viewport |
| lazy loading for non-priority images | bandwidth goes to what is visible |
| dev-mode warnings | flags missing priority on the LCP element, oversized images, missing preconnect |

### Resource hints
- {{preconnect}} to the image CDN and API origin the first view needs.
- Avoid preloading everything: each preload competes with the LCP resource.
- Defer non-critical widgets with {{@defer (on viewport)}} so their JavaScript does not delay first render.

### View Transitions API
{{provideRouter(routes, withViewTransitions())}} wraps route changes in {{document.startViewTransition}}, so the browser cross-fades between the old and new DOM. Named elements ({{view-transition-name}}) can animate between pages, for example an account card expanding into the account detail header. It is progressive enhancement: browsers without support just navigate. Respect {{prefers-reduced-motion}} and keep transitions short so they never delay interaction.

questions.q: When and how would you ship Angular components as Web Components (Angular Elements) for use in non-Angular hosts, and what goes wrong?
questions.a:
### Use cases
- Embedding a widget (payments status, FX calculator, consent banner) into a legacy page, a CMS, a React app or a partner portal.
- Gradual migration: new Angular pieces inside an old AngularJS or server-rendered application.
- A design-system component consumed by teams on different frameworks (though framework-free Web Components or Lit are often a better fit for pure UI primitives).

### How it works
{{createCustomElement(Component, { injector })}} wraps a standalone component as a custom element class; {{customElements.define('bank-fx-quote', el)}} registers it. Inputs become properties and attributes (dash-cased), outputs become DOM {{CustomEvent}}s. The host page needs only a script tag.

### Pitfalls and decisions
| Concern | Guidance |
|---|---|
| bundle size | each element bundle carries the Angular runtime; build one bundle with several elements, or share via import maps or federation |
| multiple Angular versions on one page | works only with care; prefer a single version and zoneless change detection |
| change detection | use zoneless plus signals so the element updates on input changes without Zone.js patching the host page |
| styles | ViewEncapsulation.ShadowDom isolates styles from the host; design tokens via CSS custom properties pierce the shadow boundary |
| attributes are strings | complex inputs should be set as properties from JavaScript, not attributes |
| forms and accessibility | form-associated custom elements need ElementInternals; label association across shadow DOM needs care |
| events | outputs bubble only if you dispatch with bubbles/composed; document the event contract like an API |
| versioning | the tag name plus attributes and events are a public contract; version it semantically |
pts: createCustomElement wraps a standalone component as a custom element.
Inputs are properties and attributes; outputs are CustomEvents.
Zoneless and Shadow DOM avoid fighting the host page.
Bundle size and multiple Angular versions are the main costs.
Treat the tag, attributes and events as a versioned public API.
questions.ex: A bank needed its new Angular FX quote widget inside a 12-year-old JSP online banking site and a partner's React portal. Shipping it as a zoneless, Shadow DOM custom element with a documented attribute and event contract let both hosts embed it with one script tag; bundle size was kept to 95 KB by packaging three widgets together.

questions.q: What are Angular Signal Forms, how do they differ from Reactive Forms, and how would you decide whether to adopt them in a banking application?
questions.a:
### What they are
Signal Forms (introduced as **experimental** in Angular 21, imported from {{@angular/forms/signals}}) build a form *from a signal holding your model*. You declare validation as a schema function; the form exposes field state (value, valid, errors, touched, pending) as signals. Templates bind controls to fields with a field directive. Because the API is experimental, names and shapes may still change between releases.

### Compared with Reactive Forms
| | Reactive Forms | Signal Forms |
|---|---|---|
| Source of truth | FormGroup and FormControl objects | your model signal; the form is a view over it |
| Typing | typed since v14, but nested generics get verbose | inferred from the model type |
| Reactivity | valueChanges observables | signals, compose with computed and effect |
| Validation | validator functions attached to controls | schema function with rules, conditional and async validation |
| Cross-field rules | group validators | rules that read other fields' signals |
| Maturity | stable, huge ecosystem | experimental; APIs may change |

### Adoption decision for a bank
- **New, self-contained forms** in an app already on signals and zoneless: a reasonable pilot, isolated behind a small wrapper so API changes touch one place.
- **Core flows** (payments, loan applications) and shared form libraries: stay on Reactive Forms until Signal Forms is stable; migration later is incremental, form by form.
- Whatever you use, keep **server-side validation authoritative**; client validation is user experience, not control.
pts: Form built from a model signal; field state as signals.
Schema-based validation, inferred types.
Experimental in Angular 21: pilot behind a wrapper.
Reactive Forms for core flows until stable.
Server-side validation stays authoritative.
questions.ex: A team piloted Signal Forms on an internal "change contact preferences" screen while keeping payments on Reactive Forms. They wrapped field binding in a small shared component, so when an experimental API name changed in a minor release the fix touched one file instead of every form.

questions.q: How should a frontend platform team use AI coding tools with Angular (the Angular CLI MCP server, rules files, generated code) without lowering quality or security?
questions.a:
### What exists
- The **Angular CLI MCP server** ({{ng mcp}}) lets AI assistants in editors query current Angular documentation, best practices and project information, and run CLI-backed tasks, so suggestions follow the installed Angular version instead of outdated training data.
- **Rules or instructions files** in the repository (for example a best-practices file the assistant reads) encode team conventions: standalone components, signals, new control flow, OnPush or zoneless, testing approach.
- Assistants increasingly run **migrations** (standalone, control flow, signal inputs) alongside the official schematics.

### Platform team responsibilities
| Area | Practice |
|---|---|
| grounding | enable the CLI MCP server and a repository rules file so generated code matches your Angular version and conventions |
| guardrails | the same lint rules, strict TypeScript, tests, bundle budgets and accessibility checks apply to AI-written code |
| migrations | prefer official schematics for mechanical migrations; use AI for the long tail, reviewed like any change |
| security | no secrets or customer data in prompts; approved enterprise tools only; review generated dependencies (typosquatting risk) |
| design system | expose components and tokens to the assistant (documentation, MCP) so it composes existing components rather than inventing new ones |
| measurement | track lead time, change failure rate and review load, not lines generated |

### What reviewers should watch for
Outdated patterns (NgModules, constructor injection everywhere, {{*ngIf}}), subscriptions without cleanup, direct DOM access breaking SSR, unnecessary new dependencies, missing accessibility attributes, and tests that assert implementation details.
pts: Ground assistants in the installed Angular version (CLI MCP server).
Encode conventions in a repository rules file.
Same quality gates for AI-written code.
Schematics for mechanical migrations, AI for the tail.
Measure delivery outcomes, not generated lines.

cheat:
### Core model
AOT compiles templates to instruction functions (Ivy, locality, tree-shaking, strict template type-checking). Standalone components with bootstrapApplication and provider functions; lazy loadComponent and loadChildren; route-scoped providers. Hierarchical DI: root, route environment injectors, component injectors; inject() in injection contexts; InjectionToken, multi providers, makeEnvironmentProviders.

### Change detection and signals
Zone.js triggers whole-tree checks; OnPush checks on input reference changes, events, async pipe, signal reads; zoneless (provideZonelessChangeDetection) relies on signals and explicit notifications. signal, computed (lazy, memoised), effect (side effects only), linkedSignal, untracked; immutable updates. input(), output(), model(), viewChild() and contentChild() as signals. Never fix ExpressionChanged with setTimeout: fix data flow.

### Templates
@if, @for with track by stable id (never $index for dynamic lists), @switch, @let; @defer with on viewport, interaction, idle, hover, timer, when, prefetch; placeholders with fixed size. No heavy function calls in templates: computed.

### Data and async
HttpClient with functional interceptors (correlation, CSRF or auth, retry only GETs, timeout, typed errors). RxJS: switchMap for reads, exhaustMap for submits (plus idempotency keys), concatMap for ordered writes, mergeMap with limits; share or shareReplay with refCount; WebSockets with backoff and jitter. Signals at the edges via toSignal and toObservable; resource, rxResource, httpResource for signal-driven reads. takeUntilDestroyed and DestroyRef for cleanup.

### Forms and state
Typed reactive forms, cross-field and debounced async validators (updateOn blur), server validation authoritative, server-side drafts. State: server state in resources or query caches; feature state in signal services or SignalStore at route level; NgRx Store for complex event-heavy global state.

### Performance
OnPush, signals, zoneless; virtual scrolling; per-row signals and rAF batching for live grids; web workers; budgets in angular.json; esbuild metafile analysis; NgOptimizedImage; SSR or prerendering for public pages with hydration, event replay, incremental hydration; Web Vitals RUM and Lighthouse CI.

### Security and quality
Sanitisation by default; no bypassSecurityTrust with user data; CSP nonces (ngCspNonce, CSP_NONCE), Trusted Types; BFF with HttpOnly cookies; guards are UX only. Accessibility: semantics, CDK a11y, focus management, LiveAnnouncer, axe in CI. i18n: built-in or runtime libraries, Intl formatting, locale-aware parsing. Testing: Vitest or Jest, harnesses and role queries, HttpTestingController, Playwright on Chromium and WebKit.

### Principal moves
Framework choice by consistency and skills; modular monolith before micro-frontends; strangler-by-route for AngularJS; platform with shell, design system and generators; frontend SLOs and canary releases; Web Vitals programme with team ownership; supply chain controls and PCI script monitoring; offline PWAs with encrypted queues; AI assistants via BFF with confirmable actions; component library as a product; modernisation via schematics and scorecards.

### Added diagrams to remember
- DI lookup walks element injectors, then route, then root, then platform.
- Zoneless: only signals, markForCheck and template events schedule change detection.
- Interceptor order matters: auth, correlation, retry for idempotent calls only, error mapping last.
- Router order: canMatch, lazy load, canActivate, resolver, component input binding, canDeactivate.
- SSR: HTML first, hydrate without re-render, event replay, incremental hydration of defer blocks.
